intro.html: Writers need exact words for unkindness, so that readers can tell a sharp comment from a cruel one and a quiet snub from an open insult. This topic gives you those words. Knowing them helps you name what is happening, in a story or in real life, and choose better.

Making someone seem small: belittle, demean, denigrate. Words that look down: derogatory and pejorative (a word with a negative slant). Disapproving: deprecate. Kinds of insult: an affront (open), a slight (often quiet), an aspersion (an attack on someone’s good name). And invidious: likely to stir up envy or seem unfair.
Many of these begin with de-, meaning down: they push someone down. Pejorative comes from the Latin for worse, and aspersion from a verb meaning to sprinkle, as if splashing mud on a name.

words.def: to make someone or something seem small or unimportant
words.ex: Don’t {belittle} your little brother’s drawing; he worked hard on it.
words.ctx: Rather than praise the team’s second-place finish, the coach chose to {belittle} it, calling it “just another loss” in front of the whole school.
words.etym: First used in America in the 1780s: be- (make) + little.

mn.text: Rex sneers, “Baby stuff!” at Pip’s drawing, and Pip feels about two inches tall: Rex {belittles} it.

scene.alt: A sneering man points at a boy’s drawing, and the boy shrinks to a tiny size.

words.def: to lower someone’s dignity or standing
words.ex: The coach refused to {demean} his players by yelling insults at them.
words.ctx: Forcing a worker to wear a sign reading “I was late” would {demean} anyone; the manager’s new rule was meant to embarrass, not to teach.

mn.text: Just to show who is boss, Victor makes the new worker scrub the whole floor with a toothbrush: the order is meant to {demean} him.

scene.alt: A smug boss points as a worker kneels to scrub the floor with a toothbrush.

words.ex: The referee warned the player to stop making {derogatory} comments about the other team.
words.ctx: The review was not merely critical but {derogatory}; instead of discussing the book, it called the author lazy and foolish.
words.etym: From Latin derogare, “to take away from, detract”: de- (away) + rogare (to ask).

mn.text: The rude frog croaks a nasty name at every snail that passes: “Slowpoke!” His remarks are {derogatory}.

scene.alt: A rude frog shouts “Slowpoke!” at a sad little snail.

words.def: showing disapproval; giving a word a negative slant
words.ctx: Calling the old car a “jalopy” is {pejorative}: the word makes the very same car sound shabby and worthless.

mn.text: Lila calls the sniffing puppy “curious”; Aunt Greta calls it “nosy.” Same puppy, but nosy is the {pejorative} word: it makes things sound worse.

scene.alt: A girl calls a sniffing puppy curious while a grumpy woman calls it nosy.

words.def: to criticize unfairly; to run down
words.ex: It is unkind to {denigrate} other people’s work just to make your own look better.
words.ctx: Instead of improving his own pies, the rival baker tried to {denigrate} hers, telling customers they were dry and stale, though they were nothing of the kind.

mn.text: Whatever the class paints, the jealous judge grades it down: “Ugly. Boring. F!” She {denigrates} their work.

scene.alt: A jealous judge holds up an F for a fine painting while the young painter looks hurt.

words.def: to express disapproval of; also, to play down
words.ex: The museum guide politely {deprecated} touching the paintings.
words.ctx: Though Dev had scored the winning goal, he {deprecated} his own part in the game, insisting that his teammates had done all the hard work.
words.etym: From Latin deprecari, “to pray against, to ward off”: de- (away) + precari (to pray).

mn.text: The cat sniffs the fancy new cushion, wrinkles her nose and stalks away: she {deprecates} it.

scene.alt: A cat turns up her nose at a new cushion and walks away.

words.def: an open insult; something that offends
words.ex: Arriving an hour late to his own party was an {affront} to his guests.
words.ctx: The chef took the request for ketchup as an {affront}, since she had spent all day perfecting the sauce on that very dish.
words.etym: From Old French afronter, “to strike in the face,” from Latin ad frontem (to the face).

mn.text: Right in front of everyone, Rex pushes away Nana Lou’s homemade pie and says, “Ew, no thanks!” It is an {affront}.

scene.alt: A man rudely refuses a grandmother’s homemade pie to her face, and she is shocked.

words.def: an act that shows disrespect, often by ignoring or leaving someone out
words.ex: Leaving Kai off the invitation list was a {slight} he never forgot.
words.ctx: Grandma was hurt by the {slight}: everyone else at the table was served first, and no one even asked whether she wanted dessert.
words.note: As an adjective, slight means small (a slight cold). The noun keeps the idea: a slight treats someone as small and unimportant.

mn.text: Ivy hands a party invitation to everyone in class except Kai; being left out on purpose makes him feel small. It is a {slight}.

labels.text: left OUT: made to feel SLIGHT

scene.alt: A girl hands out party invitations but skips one boy, who sits sadly alone.

words.def: an attack on someone’s good name, usually unfair
words.ex: Rex cast {aspersions} on Maya’s honesty without a shred of proof.
words.ctx: The coach refused to cast {aspersions} on the referee; instead of blaming him for the loss, she said her team simply had not played well enough.
words.etym: From Latin aspersio, “a sprinkling,” from aspergere (to sprinkle on): ad- (on) + spargere (to scatter).
words.note: The word usually comes in the phrase cast aspersions on someone.

mn.cue: a-SPERS: SPRINKLING mud on a name
mn.text: Rex flicks muddy rumors at the poster with Maya’s name on it, splattering her good name: he casts {aspersions} on her.

scene.alt: A sneaky man flicks mud at a sign with a girl’s name on it while she watches sadly.

words.def: likely to stir up envy or resentment; unfair
words.ex: It is {invidious} to compare brothers’ report cards in front of the whole family.
words.ctx: The principal refused to name a “best class,” saying such {invidious} rankings would only make the other classes feel resentful and unfairly judged.
words.etym: From Latin invidiosus, “causing envy,” from invidia (envy), from invidere (to look at with envy).

mn.text: “Why can’t you be more like your sister?” Aunt Greta asks, pointing at Ivy’s trophy while Zoe looks on: the comparison is {invidious}.

scene.alt: A woman points at one girl’s trophy and tells the other girl to be more like her sister; the second girl looks hurt.

after.cap: From quiet snubs to open insults.

after.html: deprecate (disapprove of, play down) is often confused with depreciate (lose value). A car depreciates as it ages; a modest person deprecates her own success. A slight can also be quiet: leaving someone out on purpose is a slight even if nothing is said.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: “Stubborn” is the {pejorative} word; “determined” is the kind one.

after.cap: A word with a negative slant is pejorative.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: Their new car will depreciate in value over the years.
Their new car will deprecate in value over the years.
Their new car will denigrate in value over the years.
items.why: To depreciate is to lose value. To deprecate is to disapprove of or play down, and to denigrate is to run someone down.

items.q: Which word is the pejorative one for a person who saves money carefully?
items.why: Stingy gives the same habit a negative slant; thrifty and frugal are neutral or kind.

items.q: True or false: a slight can happen without a single word being said.
items.why: True. Leaving someone out or ignoring them on purpose is a slight, even in silence.

items.q: To “cast aspersions” on someone is to…
items.why: An aspersion is a damaging, usually unfair, remark about someone’s character. The Latin root means to sprinkle, as if splashing mud.
